hints: Start by drawing trichloroethene, $\text{CCl}_2=\text{CHCl}$, and remember addition across the $\text{C=C}$ will give a saturated product to test for chirality.
Recall a chiral carbon needs four different groups attached, so look for a product carbon with H, halogen and carbon all different and no duplicate $\text{Cl}$ atoms on the same carbon.
Add each reagent across the double bond on paper and check which addition creates a carbon with four unique substituents.
walkthrough:
**Draw the starting alkene**

Think of trichloroethene as an ethene with three H atoms replaced by Cl.

Its structure is:
$$\text{Cl}_2\text{C}=\text{CHCl}$$

**Recall the test for a chiral product**

A molecule is chiral if it has a carbon with four different groups attached and no plane of symmetry.

So after addition, we need a $\text{C}$ bonded to four different things, which means we must avoid $\text{C}$ atoms with two identical atoms like $\text{CCl}_2$ or $\text{CH}_2$.

**Add bromine and check**

Bromine adds across the double bond by electrophilic addition:
$$\text{Cl}_2\text{C}=\text{CHCl} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CCl}_2\text{Br}-\text{CHClBr}$$
Now look at the right-hand carbon. It is bonded to H, Cl, Br and $\text{CCl}_2\text{Br}$. That is four different groups, so it is a chiral centre and the product is chiral.

options.A: Addition of $\text{Br}_2$ gives $\text{CHClBr}-\text{CCl}_2\text{Br}$ (1,2-dibromo-1,1,2-trichloroethane). The $\text{CHClBr}$ carbon is attached to H, Cl, Br and $\text{CCl}_2\text{Br}$, four different groups, so it is chiral. The product is formed as a racemic mixture but is chiral.
options.B: Addition of HCl gives a tetrachloroethane, either $\text{CCl}_3-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ or $\text{CHCl}_2-\text{CCl}_2\text{H}$. The first has a $\text{CCl}_3$ carbon and a $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ carbon, the second has two $\text{CHCl}_2$ type carbons with two identical Cl atoms. No carbon has four different groups, so the product is achiral.
options.C: Cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$, is a nucleophile for substitution, not electrophilic addition to this electron-poor $\text{C=C}$ bond. Even if addition or substitution occurred, it would not generate the required $\text{C}$ with four different substituents in the same clean way as bromine addition. Students choosing this may confuse alkene addition with nitrile formation from halogenoalkanes.
options.D: NaOH provides $\text{OH}^-$, which causes substitution or elimination, not simple addition to give a chiral saturated halide. Any substitution product from trichloroethene would still contain $\text{CCl}_2$ or $\text{C=O}$ type achiral groupings. Students choosing this may be thinking of hydrolysis to an alcohol without checking the chirality condition.
